Vertebrate

/VER-tuh-brate/ — rhymes with PERT-uh-brate · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A vertebrate is an animal that has a backbone and an internal skeleton, such as a fish, bird, reptile, or mammal.

A frog is a vertebrate; its tiny backbone shows clearly on the X-ray.

Worked Example

When the paleontologist carefully brushed away the rock, a delicate backbone of a vertebrate creature from millions of years ago came into view.

Vertebrate is more precise than just 'animal' because it specifies a key biological feature—the internal backbone and skeletal structure—that distinguishes vertebrates from invertebrates.

How Vertebrate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

animal

animal: a living creature that moves and feeds, not a plant

organism

organism: any single living thing, large or small

creature

creature: any living being, especially an animal

Antonyms

invertebrate

invertebrate: an animal that has no backbone, like a worm

mollusk

mollusk: a soft-bodied, backbone-less animal such as a snail

How Strong Is It? — being → organism → animal → vertebrate

being vs. vertebrate

being vs. vertebrate: A being is the broadest word of all, naming any living thing at all, while a vertebrate is far more specific, naming only creatures that have a backbone.

organism vs. vertebrate

organism vs. vertebrate: An organism is any single living thing, from bacteria to whales, but a vertebrate narrows that huge group down to those with an internal spine.

animal vs. vertebrate

animal vs. vertebrate: Animal is broader than vertebrate: every vertebrate is an animal, yet many animals, like worms and insects, are not vertebrates because they lack a backbone.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of vertebrate.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vertebr-

Root — vertebr-: backbone; joint of the spine (from Latin 'vertere', to turn) (Latin)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: having or characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: The root 'vertebr-' means backbone and the suffix '-ate' means 'having,' so a vertebrate is literally an animal 'having a backbone' — an internal spine built of linked, turning joints.

Use the root in a new word: invertebrate

Use the root in a new word: invertebrate: A jellyfish is an invertebrate: the prefix 'in-' (not) plus the same 'vertebr-' root shows it has no backbone, the exact reverse of a vertebrate.

Root Check

Word Choice

scientific / neutral

Use vertebrate in science, biology, and zoology when classifying animals by their internal skeleton. In casual speech you'd just say 'animal,' but for homework or tests, vertebrate is the precise, academic term.
